title: How To Handle The “Cool” Kids
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses a subtle bias he sees in many classrooms: teachers unconsciously favoring socially influential 'cool' students by extending extra chances, mimicking their style, or showing visible admiration. He argues this favoritism is deeply corrosive to classroom morale, breeding resentment and distrust among the rest of the class. His remedy has three parts: following the classroom management plan identically for every student, including popular ones, so the class sees consequences enforced without favoritism; refusing to be personally impressed by trends, status symbols, or social media culture; and prioritizing consistent warmth toward the whole class over individualized relationship-building with a few students. He closes by connecting this to a broader principle of maintaining a steady, professional presence rather than trying to be liked or 'cool' — a posture that ultimately earns more respect from all students, including the popular ones.
points: Teachers can unconsciously favor socially influential 'cool' students, which is one of the most corrosive forms of perceived unfairness in a classroom.
Enforcing the classroom management plan identically for popular and unpopular students alike proves to the class that there is no favoritism.
Teachers should refuse to be personally impressed by student status symbols, trends, or social media influence.
Consistent day-to-day kindness toward the whole class builds more trust than individualized relationship-building with a few standout students.
Maintaining a steady, professional, non-'cool' presence ultimately earns more respect than trying to mimic or please popular students.
quotes: Nothing is more hurtful to the rest of the class. Nothing makes students more resentful and less trusting than the teacher who obviously likes some students better than others.
They must see you follow your classroom management plan the same with every student. When a “cool” student breaks a rule, it’s a great opportunity to show your class that you can be trusted.
Refuse to play into the social media culture that says that some people are more special or worthy of our attention than others.
Jordan’s are just shoes. A haircut is just one of many styles. Looking out for your neighbor is cool and humbleness is a virtue.
Your consistent day-after-day kindness and pleasantness is much more influential than trying to build relationships one student at a time. Focus on your class as a whole.

Be the same steady presence and trust and respect will come readily. Your likability will soar among all and the cool kids will feel wonderfully knocked down a peg and free to be just regular, humble, and valued members of the class.
